from setuptools import setup, find_packages

setup(
    name="files-context-construction",
    version="0.1.0",
    description="Meltano Cloud industry context for construction: datasets for AI assistants and analysts.",
    packages=find_packages(),
    # bundle/ is copied verbatim into the workspace repository; ship every file under it
    include_package_data=True,

version: datasets/v0.3
title: "Construction: modelling it in dbt"
questions: How should raw construction data be modelled in dbt so that it reconciles?
description: |
  Conventions for building dbt models on raw construction data. They apply on top of the workspace's
  usual dbt layout: staging, then intermediate, then marts.

  ## Projects and cost codes

  - **Conform cost codes.** Each project, and each source system, can use its own codes. Build a
    mapping seed or table from source codes to a standard structure in an intermediate model, and
    test that every cost code is mapped.
  - **Keep the project key consistent.** The ERP, the project management tool and the scheduler each
    have their own project IDs. Build a `dim_project` with a crosswalk of every source's ID.
  - **Separate cost types** (labour, plant, materials, subcontract, preliminaries, overhead) as a
    column, not as separate models, so they sum to the project total.

  ## Money

  - **Never use floating point for money.** Use `numeric`/`decimal`.
  - **Gross, net and retention are different amounts.** Keep gross valuation, retention, previous
    certified and amount due as separate columns, as the valuation document shows them. Do not
    derive one from another unless the source does not provide it.
  - **Cumulative to-date figures are common.** Valuations and CVRs are often reported as totals to
    date. Derive the period movement as this period's to-date − last period's, and test it is not
    negative unless a credit was issued.
  - Keep VAT (including the UK construction reverse charge) and the Construction Industry Scheme
    (CIS) deductions as separate columns from the net amount.

  ## Periods and versions

  - Use the organisation's **financial period calendar** (often 4-4-5 or month-end cut-offs), not
    calendar months, for CVR and valuation reporting.
  - **Snapshot each month's forecast and budget** (`fct_cost_value_reconciliation_monthly`) rather
    than overwrite. Margin movement and forecast accuracy need the history.
  - **Programmes have baselines.** Keep the baseline and each revision of programme activities, and
    compare forecast dates with the baseline, not with the previous revision only.
  - Costs are posted late: model cost transactions incrementally on a stable ID and reprocess a
    look-back window around period close.

  ## Tests

  Add these beside the usual `unique` and `not_null` tests:

  - **Cost reconciliation:** project cost by period equals the general ledger's work-in-progress
    postings for the same project and period.
  - **Mapping coverage:** every cost transaction maps to a standard cost code.
  - **Valuation consistency:** amount due = gross value − retention − previously certified.
  - **Commitment cover:** cost against a subcontract does not exceed its committed value plus
    approved variations, or is flagged.
  - **Accepted values** on cost types, variation statuses and incident types.
  - **Freshness** on timesheet and cost sources before month-end close.

  ## Naming

  - Prefix models by layer (`stg_`, `int_`, `fct_`, `dim_`), and name facts for their grain:
    `fct_project_costs`, `fct_valuations`, `fct_variations`, `fct_programme_activities`.

  ## Sensitive columns

  Tag personal columns (worker names, contact details, health and incident details) in the model
  YAML (for example `meta: {pii: true}`) and keep them out of marts that do not need them. See
  *Construction: handling the data*.

version: datasets/v0.3
title: "Construction: data model"
questions: What are the core entities of construction data, and at what grain should each be modelled?
description: |
  The entities most construction data reduces to, with the grain and key of each. Use it to map raw
  source tables onto a consistent model. Names are suggestions; keep the organisation's own terms
  where they already exist.

  | Entity | Grain (one row per…) | Notes |
  |---|---|---|
  | `project` (job, contract) | project | Client, contract form (for example JCT or NEC), contract value, start and completion dates, status |
  | `cost_code` | code in the cost structure | Hierarchical (WBS): trade, element or package. Map each project's codes to a standard structure |
  | `budget_line` | project per cost code per budget version | Original budget, approved changes, current budget. Version it |
  | `commitment` (subcontract, purchase order) | order or subcontract line | Supplier, cost code, committed value. Increases with approved variations |
  | `cost_transaction` | posting to a project cost code | Labour, plant, materials, subcontract or overhead. Date incurred and date posted |
  | `valuation` (application for payment) | application per period | Gross value of work done to date, retention held, amount certified, amount paid |
  | `variation` (change order, compensation event) | change | Raised, priced, agreed or rejected, with value and time impact |
  | `forecast` (cost value reconciliation, CVR) | project per cost code per month | Cost to date, cost to complete, forecast final cost, forecast final value |
  | `programme_activity` | activity per programme revision | Planned and actual start and finish, percent complete, baseline dates |
  | `timesheet` (labour entry) | worker per project per day | Hours by cost code, trade, rate |
  | `plant_hire` | hire period | Item, supplier, on-hire and off-hire dates, rate |
  | `site` | site or plot | For housebuilders, a `plot` with house type and build stage sits under the site |
  | `incident` | incident or near miss | Type, severity, whether reportable, date, site, contractor involved |
  | `defect` (snag) | defect | Location, trade responsible, raised and closed dates |

  ## Relationships

  - A **project** has a **budget** by **cost code**, and **commitments** and **cost transactions**
    against those codes.
  - A **commitment** to a subcontractor produces **valuations** from that subcontractor, and the
    project produces valuations to the client.
  - **Variations** change both the budget (cost) and the contract value (revenue).
  - A monthly **forecast** brings budget, commitments, costs and valuations together per cost code.

  ## Status and history

  Budgets, forecasts, programmes and contract values change every month. Keep each period's version
  (the month-end CVR, the programme baseline and each revision), because margin and progress reports
  compare this month with last month and with the original tender.

# files-context-construction

A Meltano [file bundle](https://docs.meltano.com/concepts/plugins/#file-bundles) of **industry
context for construction**. Meltano Cloud adds it to a workspace whose organisation's industry
is Construction.

The bundle holds datasets with no query. Each one is a written briefing: the segments and source
systems of the industry, its core entities, the metrics it runs on, how to model its data in dbt,
and how to handle its data. They are written for an AI assistant (or an analyst) working in the
workspace, for example one building dbt models on raw construction data.

```
analyze/datasets/construction/
  overview.yml
  data-model.yml
  metrics.yml
  dbt-modelling.yml
  data-handling.yml
```

## Organisation knowledge: `#organisation-context`

Every dataset here is tagged `#organisation-context`, the tag of an organisation's knowledge in Meltano
Cloud. The `get_organisation_knowledge` MCP tool returns the full text of every dataset with it, for an
AI assistant to read before it models, transforms or queries the workspace's data. In the repository,
`grep -rl '#organisation-context' analyze/datasets` finds the same set. Tag a dataset of your own the
same way to add it.

## Install

Meltano Cloud installs it when Construction is chosen as the workspace's industry, in the
setup wizard or with the `set_organisation_context` MCP tool.

In a Meltano project of your own, save this definition to a file outside the project, for example
`/tmp/files-context-construction.yml`:

```yaml
name: files-context-construction
namespace: files_context_construction
variant: matatika
pip_url: git+https://github.com/meltano/files-context-construction.git@v0.1.0
update:
  '*.yml': true
```

then add the bundle from the project directory. `meltano add` writes the datasets; a plain
`meltano install` does not:

```sh
meltano add --plugin-type files files-context-construction --from-ref /tmp/files-context-construction.yml
```

`update: '*.yml': true` lets `meltano upgrade files` refresh the datasets from a newer version.

## Release

Tag a version (`git tag -a v0.1.0 -m v0.1.0 && git push --tags`) and bump the `pip_url` ref in the
Meltano Cloud registry definition (`plugins/files/files-context-construction--matatika.yml`).

These datasets are general industry context, not legal, regulatory, health and safety or financial advice.

version: datasets/v0.3
title: "Construction: industry overview"
questions: What does a construction organisation's data look like, and where does it come from?
description: |
  Industry context for this workspace, for the people and AI assistants working in it. It has no
  query: it is a briefing to read before modelling or analysing this organisation's data.

  ## Segments

  Construction covers organisations that design, build, maintain and supply the built environment.
  The segments differ in which entities and metrics matter most:

  - **Main contractors:** run projects for a client and subcontract most of the work. Contracts,
    budgets, cost codes, valuations, variations and subcontractor payments drive the data.
  - **Specialist and trade subcontractors:** mechanical and electrical, groundworks, steel, fit-out.
    Labour hours, plant, materials, applications for payment and retentions drive the data.
  - **Housebuilders and developers:** land, plots, build stages, sales reservations and completions.
    Plot-level costs and build programme drive the data.
  - **Civil engineering and infrastructure:** roads, rail, water and energy works, often under
    frameworks with public clients. Long programmes, earned value and compensation events drive the
    data.
  - **Repairs, maintenance and facilities:** reactive and planned jobs against an asset register.
    Work orders, response times and first-time fix drive the data.
  - **Materials and plant hire:** builders' merchants, manufacturers and hire firms. Orders, deliveries,
    hire periods and utilisation drive the data.

  ## Typical source systems

  | System | Examples | What it holds |
  |---|---|---|
  | Construction ERP / job costing | COINS, Sage 200 or Sage Intacct Construction, Viewpoint Vista, Eque2, CMiC | Contracts, cost codes, budgets, commitments, actual costs, valuations |
  | Project management | Procore, Autodesk Construction Cloud, Oracle Aconex, Viewpoint Field View | RFIs, submittals, drawings, snags, site diaries, inspections |
  | Scheduling | Oracle Primavera P6, Microsoft Project, Asta Powerproject | Programme activities, baselines, progress, critical path |
  | Estimating | CostX, Causeway Estimating, Candy | Bills of quantities, rates, tender prices |
  | Health and safety | Procore Safety, Evotix, an in-house incident log | Incidents, near misses, inspections, permits |
  | Time and workforce | Site access and induction systems (often biometric turnstiles), CSCS Smart Check, timesheet apps | Who was on site, hours worked, competences |
  | Plant and telematics | Hire firm portals, machine telematics | Hire periods, hours, idle time, fuel |
  | Accounting / ERP | Sage, Xero, Microsoft Dynamics 365, SAP | General ledger, invoices, payroll |
  | CRM and sales (housebuilding) | Salesforce, Microsoft Dynamics 365, housebuilder sales and plot management systems | Leads, reservations, completions |

  ## What makes the data different

  - **The project is the unit.** Almost every cost, hour and document belongs to a project, and is
    broken down by a cost code structure (often a work breakdown structure, WBS) that differs by
    organisation and sometimes by project.
  - **Money moves in stages.** Costs are budgeted, committed, incurred, valued and paid at different
    times. Valuations, variations, retentions and final accounts make "what did it cost" a question
    with several answers, each correct as at a date.
  - **Forecasts matter as much as actuals.** Cost to complete and forecast final cost are monthly
    judgements by the commercial team; keep each month's forecast, not only the latest.
  - **Health and safety data is critical.** Incidents are reported to regulators and drive decisions
    on site. See *Construction: handling the data*.

  Related datasets: *data model*, *metrics*, *modelling it in dbt*, *handling the data*.

  #construction #organisation-context

version: datasets/v0.3
title: "Construction: handling the data"
questions: What care does construction data need in the warehouse?
description: |
  Construction data holds personal data about a large, mobile workforce, health and safety records,
  and commercially sensitive contract figures. These are general practices for a warehouse holding
  it. They are not legal or compliance advice: the organisation decides what applies to it.

  ## Classify the data

  | Class | Examples | Handling |
  |---|---|---|
  | Worker identity and right to work | Name, date of birth, National Insurance number, passport and visa details, CSCS card number | Restrict to HR and compliance roles. Do not load document images; keep the check result and expiry date |
  | Health and incident data | Injury details, occupational health assessments, drug and alcohol test results | Special category data under UK GDPR. Restrict tightly; report incident counts, not individuals |
  | Biometric data | Fingerprint or face templates from site access systems | **Do not load it into the warehouse.** Load only the access events it produces |
  | Location data | Site access logs, vehicle and plant tracking | Restrict access; aggregate for productivity and utilisation reporting |
  | Commercial data | Tender prices, rates, margins, subcontract values, claims | Restrict to commercial roles. Tender data is especially sensitive before contract award |
  | Supplier tax data | CIS verification numbers, UTRs, bank details | Restrict to finance roles. Mask outside payment models |

  ## Practices

  - **Least privilege.** Separate raw, staging and mart schemas, and grant raw schemas only to the
    pipelines and the people who maintain them. Restrict by project where joint ventures or clients
    must not see each other's data.
  - **Mask by default.** Hash or mask worker identifiers in shared marts, and give unmasked access by
    role.
  - **No production data in development** without masking.
  - **Keep safety records whole.** Load incident and inspection records append-only and keep their
    history; they may be needed for investigations and claims years later.
  - **Retention.** Contract records, health and safety records and building safety information are
    often kept for many years after completion. Agree retention periods with the organisation, and
    keep personal data no longer than needed.
  - **Data subject requests.** Under GDPR and UK GDPR a worker can ask for their data or for its
    erasure, so know where each person's data lives.

  ## Regulators and rules to be aware of

  Which apply depends on the organisation's country and activities. Common ones:

  - **UK:** UK GDPR; the Health and Safety Executive (HSE), the Construction (Design and Management)
    Regulations 2015 (CDM) and RIDDOR incident reporting; the Building Safety Act 2022 and its
    "golden thread" of building information for higher-risk buildings; HMRC's Construction Industry
    Scheme (CIS); right-to-work checks.
  - **EU:** GDPR and national health and safety regulators.
  - **US:** OSHA recordkeeping and reporting, and state privacy and biometric laws (for example
    Illinois' BIPA).
  - **Public sector clients** often add contract requirements on data, security and reporting, such as
    the UK Cyber Essentials scheme.

version: datasets/v0.3
title: "Construction: key metrics"
questions: Which metrics does a construction organisation run on, and how is each calculated?
description: |
  Standard definitions of the metrics construction organisations report. Confirm each one with the
  commercial or finance team before building it: organisations differ on what counts as cost,
  when a variation is recognised, and whether figures include retention.

  ## Commercial and margin

  | Metric | Definition |
  |---|---|
  | Contract value | Original contract sum + agreed variations. Say whether unagreed variations are included |
  | Gross margin | (Forecast final value − forecast final cost) ÷ forecast final value |
  | Margin movement | This month's forecast margin − last month's (or tender margin). A falling margin is the early warning |
  | Cost to complete | Forecast final cost − cost to date |
  | Over/under-valuation | Value recognised − value certified by the client. Large over-valuation is a cash risk |
  | Work in progress (WIP) | Cost incurred + margin recognised − amounts invoiced |

  ## Earned value (programme and cost)

  | Metric | Definition |
  |---|---|
  | Planned value (PV) | Budgeted cost of work scheduled to date |
  | Earned value (EV) | Budgeted cost of work actually completed to date |
  | Actual cost (AC) | Cost actually incurred for the work completed |
  | Cost performance index (CPI) | EV ÷ AC. Below 1 is over budget |
  | Schedule performance index (SPI) | EV ÷ PV. Below 1 is behind programme |
  | Estimate at completion (EAC) | Budget at completion ÷ CPI, or AC + remaining work at budget. State the method |

  ## Cash

  | Metric | Definition |
  |---|---|
  | Retention held | Retention deducted from valuations and not yet released, by project |
  | Debtor days | Trade receivables ÷ revenue × days in the period |
  | Payment performance | Share of supplier invoices paid within agreed terms, and average days to pay (UK large firms report this under the payment practices reporting regulations) |
  | Cash position by project | Cash received − cash paid out, per project |

  ## Delivery

  | Metric | Definition |
  |---|---|
  | Programme slippage | Forecast completion date − contractual (or baseline) completion date, in days or weeks |
  | Variation rate | Value of agreed variations ÷ original contract sum |
  | Defects per unit | Defects raised at handover ÷ units (plots, rooms or floors) handed over |
  | Labour productivity | Output (value or quantity installed) ÷ labour hours |
  | Plant utilisation | Hours worked ÷ hours on hire |

  ## Health and safety

  | Metric | Definition |
  |---|---|
  | Accident frequency rate (AFR) | Reportable incidents × 100,000 ÷ hours worked. Organisations also use per 1,000,000 hours: say which |
  | Lost time injury frequency rate (LTIFR) | Lost time injuries × 1,000,000 ÷ hours worked |
  | Near-miss reporting rate | Near misses reported ÷ hours worked (or per 100,000 hours). Higher often means a better reporting culture |
  | RIDDOR reportable incidents | Count of incidents reported to the HSE under RIDDOR (UK) |

  #construction #organisation-context
